title: Why Landmines Are The Deadliest Legacy Of War
summary: Josh and Chuck explain landmines: their scale (millions laid yearly, over 100 million in roughly 70 countries, long-lasting civilian casualties), origins in the American Civil War (Gabriel Rains and his Rains patent, "torpedoes"), use in World War I and II, Egypt's leftover World War II mines, the main types (blast, bounding/Bouncing Betty, fragmentation, cluster, anti-tank), the Belleville spring trigger, the M14 and M16 mines, the Ottawa-style treaty banning landmines and its Nobel Prize, US non-signatory status and the DMZ justification, cluster bomb treaty, and demining methods (probing, dogs, rats, bees, metal detectors, GPR, Panther and Aardvark machines, mine-clearing drones). Ends with Princess Diana's advocacy and listener mail.

segments.title: Opening banter and landmine overview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about the Atlanta weather and Easter, then introduce landmines as an overlooked global problem. They cite the scale of the issue: millions laid yearly and over 100 million in about 70 countries, with clearance pace too slow to keep up.

segments.title: Civilian casualties and leftover unexploded ordnance
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how landmines are indiscriminate and persist long after conflicts end, killing civilians disproportionately, with most recent civilian deaths being children. They mention unexploded World War II ordnance in Okinawa and roughly 100 tons of WWI-era ordnance found yearly in Belgium.

segments.title: Origins in the American Civil War
segments.summary: Landmines started in the American Civil War, when Gabriel Rains, a North Carolinian who first fought for the Union, developed and patented an early land mine, the Rains patent. Called torpedoes or subterra shells, they surprised and angered Union troops and generals, who considered them a cheap, dirty tactic. Confederate leaders were hesitant but eventually adopted them, and mines were booby-trapped in flour sacks or tied to tools. Some were still being found in Alabama in the 1960s.

segments.title: World War I and II use and strategic purpose
segments.summary: Landmines became prominent in World War I and especially World War II. The hosts explain their strategic uses: channeling or rerouting troops and tanks and slowing enemies until reinforcements arrive. Egypt has an estimated 23 million unexploded mines left from World War II fighting in the North African theater.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Sponsor break before the discussion of mine types.

segments.title: Types of anti-personnel mines
segments.summary: The hosts describe the two main groups of mines, anti-personnel and anti-tank, which both detonate under pressure. Anti-personnel types include blast mines (meant to maim), bounding or Bouncing Betty mines (which pop up and explode at chest height to kill), fragmentation mines like the Claymore, and cluster munitions that leave duds that become de facto mines.

segments.title: M14 and M16 mines and the Belleville spring trigger
segments.summary: The M14 is a small, cheap US-developed blast mine, roughly three dollars to make, that triggers with about 20 pounds of pressure and is nicknamed toe popper. The M16 is a larger bounding/fragmentation mine with cast iron housing and about a pound of TNT that pops up about three feet before exploding. Both use a Belleville spring to hold the firing pin until pressure overcomes it. The hosts discuss whether soldiers can stand on a mine after hearing a click, which they found not to be the case.

segments.title: Anti-tank mines
segments.summary: Anti-tank mines are much larger and need several pounds of pressure, typically aimed at disabling tanks by blowing off their tracks. They are often surrounded by anti-personnel mines to deter removal. One described holds about 23 pounds of explosive composition B.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Sponsor break before the segment on treaties and removal.

segments.title: International landmine treaty and US position
segments.summary: The International Campaign to Ban Landmines formed and helped create the international treaty banning production, stockpiling, and transfer of landmines, which won a Nobel Prize. About 164 countries have signed. The US and Cuba are among the few Western-leaning holdouts; the US says it needs mines for the DMZ between North and South Korea, which the hosts question. The US is still a leader in funding clearance. The US stockpile is about three million, and it has not laid mines since about 2003 in Iraq. Cluster bomb policy is also discussed, including Pentagon reasoning about a one percent failure rate and a possible ground war with North Korea.

segments.title: Mine detection and clearance methods
segments.summary: The hosts survey demining methods: probing with sticks or bayonets, trained dogs, rats, honey bees trained on TNT, metal detectors (which give false hits and miss plastic mines), ground penetrating radar developed at Ohio State University, and heavy machines like the Aardvark, Panther, and burm processing assembly. Mine-clearing drones developed by Massud Hasani are described as cheap alternatives. Casualties fell to about 3,450 in 2013 after a 1999 peak of 9,228 but rose to 8,605 in 2016, linked to Yemen and Syria. ISIS has reportedly dug up and replanted old mines in Egypt, and IEDs are compared to landmines. Princess Diana's landmine advocacy is discussed.

segments.title: Listener mail: brother and sister listening pair
segments.summary: Melissa writes about discovering the show with her brother Michael, sharing a childhood story about photographing a body pulled from a ravine, and noting she teaches kindergarten. Josh and Chuck respond and give contact information.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and provide social media and email contact details.
